name: exiftool
one_line: read and write meta information in files
plain: `exiftool` reads the hidden label attached to a file: camera model, GPS position, author, software, creation time, comments, thumbnails and more. Photos, PDFs, Office documents, audio, video and many other formats carry this metadata.

In forensics and CTFs a flag or a clue is often in the metadata: a comment field, a GPS coordinate, an odd author, an embedded thumbnail, a mismatched file type. exiftool also writes metadata, which lets you scrub files or craft test files.
It reads over 400 formats and prints each tag with its group, so you can see where a value came from.
when: First look at an image, PDF or document in a forensics challenge.
Find where a photo was taken (GPS) or what device took it.
See who created a document and with which software.
Check whether a file's real type matches its extension.
Remove metadata before sharing a file, or edit it.

examples.title: Show everything in a file
examples.explain: Lists every tag it can read. Read the Comment, Author, GPS, Software and Create Date lines first.

examples.title: Show tags with their group names
examples.explain: -G1 prints the group (EXIF, XMP, IPTC...), -a shows duplicate tags, -s uses short tag names. You can see which block holds each value.

examples.title: Read just a few tags
examples.explain: Naming tags prints only those. Handy for scripts.

examples.title: A whole folder as a table
examples.explain: -csv writes a spreadsheet row per file. -r descends into subfolders.

examples.title: Find GPS in decimal
examples.explain: -n prints raw numbers instead of formatted text, so you can paste the coordinates into a map.

examples.title: Search for files by a tag value
examples.explain: -if keeps only files whose tag matches an expression.

examples.title: Look at hidden text
examples.explain: Common places where challenge authors hide a message or flag.

examples.title: Extract the embedded thumbnail
examples.explain: -b outputs the raw binary. The thumbnail can show a different picture than the main image, which is a classic forensics clue.

examples.title: Wipe all metadata
examples.explain: Setting a tag to nothing deletes it. -all= removes every writable tag. A backup photo.jpg_original is kept unless you add -overwrite_original.

examples.title: Write a tag
examples.explain: Adds or changes a tag. Useful to build test files for a forensics lab.

examples.title: Check the real file type
examples.explain: exiftool recognises the format by its content, not its name, so it exposes a renamed file.

examples.title: Dump everything as JSON
examples.explain: Structured output for scripts and jq.

mistakes: Forgetting that exiftool keeps a backup: file.jpg_original appears. Use -overwrite_original if you do not want it.
Believing the file extension: exiftool reports the real type, so a mismatch is a clue.
Reading only the default output: add -a -G1 -u and -v to see everything, including unknown tags.
Copying a photo to chat apps and expecting GPS to stay: many apps strip it.
Using -all= and thinking the picture is anonymous: image content and filename can still identify a place or person.
try: Run exiftool on a downloaded image and write down the Software and Comment lines.
Extract the thumbnail with -b -ThumbnailImage and compare it with the original.
Turn the GPS position into decimal with -n and paste it into a map.
Scrub a copy of the file with -all= and compare with the original using diff.

captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
